title: Keeping internet freedom code and releases reachable
description:
ForkMesh keeps Git repositories, releases and downloads reachable when a host is blocked or a project is taken down, using signed, integrity-checked mirrors run by independent hosts. We are applying to the Open Technology Fund and want to build what developers of internet freedom tools actually need, so we are asking the people who build and run them.

It takes about 10 minutes. Only the first question is required; skip anything you prefer not to answer.

You do not need to name yourself, your project or your country. Regions are enough. Answers are stored sealed, only the ForkMesh team reads them, and we publish only anonymized summaries.
thankYou: Thank you. Your answers shape what we build and what we ask the Open Technology Fund to fund. If you left a way to reach you, we will follow up within a week. Questions: hello@forkmesh.com.

questions.title: Which best describes your work?
options: I build or maintain a censorship circumvention tool
I build or maintain another privacy or security tool
I work at an internet freedom or digital rights organization
I run servers, mirrors or infrastructure for others
I research censorship or measure networks
I use these tools but do not build them
Other

questions.title: How many people work on your project or team?
options: Just me
2 to 5
6 to 20
More than 20
I am not part of a project

questions.title: Where are the people who use your software?

options: Northern Africa
Sub-Saharan Africa
Latin America and the Caribbean
Northern America
Central Asia
Eastern Asia
South-eastern Asia
Southern Asia
Western Asia (including the Middle East)
Eastern Europe (including Russia)
Northern, Southern and Western Europe
Oceania
Worldwide or I don't know

questions.title: Where do your code and releases live today?
options: GitHub
GitLab.com
Codeberg or another Forgejo or Gitea host
SourceHut
Our own Git server
App stores (Google Play, App Store, F-Droid)
Our own website or download server
Telegram, email or file-sharing channels
Other

questions.title: In the last two years, which of these has happened to your project or its users?
options: Our repository or account was suspended or taken down by the host
Our code host (GitHub, GitLab or another) was blocked where our users are
Our website or download server was blocked (DNS, IP or SNI filtering)
A release or app was removed from an app store
Users downloaded a fake or tampered copy
Our domain was seized, suspended or lost under pressure
A mirror went stale or offline when we needed it
Team members lost access because of sanctions or trade restrictions
None of these

questions.title: Tell us about the worst of these. What happened, how long did it last, and how did it affect your users?
questions.help: Leave out names, places or details that could identify you or anyone else.

questions.title: How serious is losing access to your code or releases for your project?
questions.help: 1 is not a problem for us, 5 is critical.

questions.title: What do you do today when your code or downloads are blocked or taken down?
options: Keep copies on other Git hosts
Run our own mirrors or download servers
Post releases on Telegram or other channels
Use a CDN or domain fronting
Ask users to reach us through a VPN or Tor
Share through torrents or IPFS
We have no plan yet
Other

questions.title: Where does that approach fall short? How much time or money does it cost you each month?
When your usual download is blocked, how do your users find a working copy, and how do they know it is genuine?
Which of these would help your project most?
options: Mirrors that follow our GitHub or GitLab repository automatically
Releases and binaries served from many independent mirrors
Signed releases and checksums users can check before installing
A way for users to find working mirrors when the main site is blocked
Issues and pull requests that survive an account suspension
Running our own mirror on a cheap server
Mirrors run by trusted partner organizations
Reaching mirrors over Tor or other circumvention transports
Other

questions.title: Would you keep your current code host if you added a mirror network?
options: Yes, we need to stay where we are, mirrors would be a backup
We would keep it but move releases and downloads to mirrors
We would move most of our work
Not sure

questions.title: Which threats worry you most for your code and releases?
options: Blocking of our host (DNS, IP or SNI)
Takedown of our account or repository
A malicious mirror serving tampered code or binaries
A compromised maintainer account or signing key
Leaks of who downloads or contributes (metadata)
Someone impersonating our project or maintainers
Legal pressure on hosts or mirror operators
Other

questions.title: Before trusting a new tool with your releases, what would you need to see?
options: A published independent security audit
Established, reviewed cryptography
A clear, published threat model
Open source code we can read and build
Reproducible builds
Projects we know already using it
Running it ourselves without depending on ForkMesh servers
Other

Would your team run its own ForkMesh mirror?
options: Yes, on a server we already have

Only if a partner organization runs it for us
No
Not sure

questions.title: How much could you spend each month on a server for it?
options: Nothing, it has to be free

More than $50
A partner or funder would pay

options: A Docker Compose file
A single install script

A security hardening guide

Other

options: Yes, the desktop app
Yes, the website or web dashboard
Yes, I cloned or downloaded from a ForkMesh mirror
Yes, the iPhone or Android app
Not yet

questions.title: If you tried it: how easy was it to get started?
questions.help: 1 is very hard, 5 is very easy. Skip if you have not tried it.

questions.title: If you tried it: how reliable was it?
questions.help: 1 is very unreliable, 5 is very reliable. Skip if you have not tried it.

questions.title: If you tried it: what broke, confused you, or was missing?
How likely are you to use ForkMesh for your project in the next six months?
questions.help: 1 is very unlikely, 5 is very likely.

questions.title: Could you help us test ForkMesh from a network where censorship happens?
questions.help: We agree safety rules with every tester first, and no test should put anyone at risk.
options: Yes, I can test it myself
Yes, I can introduce a partner who could
No
Not sure

questions.title: Would you be open to any of these?
options: A 30-minute interview
Piloting ForkMesh mirroring for our project
Hosting an independent mirror for other projects
Reviewing ForkMesh's threat model or cryptography
A short letter of support for our Open Technology Fund proposal
None right now

questions.title: If you would like us to follow up, how can we reach you?
questions.help: An email, Signal, Matrix or other handle. Leave it blank to stay anonymous. Add your project's name or link too if you are comfortable.
